To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a mutation in a human intellectual disability gene (GluK6) leads to a transient reduction in synaptic transmission at a critical time of development; and 2) this reduction in synaptic strength impacts on the proper formation (maturation) of hippocampal neural circuits.

the absence of GluK2 in mice results in a transient reduction of AMPA-mediated synaptic transmission and a deficit of morphological maturation at the mf-CA3 synaptic circuit, which is associated with intellectual disability.

a mutation in a mouse model of intellectual disability leads to a transient reduction in synaptic strength during postnat development, which impacts on the proper formation and function of neural circuits involved in learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular and cellular basis of intellectual disability, and more particularly, the role of the kainate receptors in the maturation of hippocampus-dependent learning and memory.
the mechanisms of synaptic plasticity, and more specifically with the role of the glutamate receptor subunit Gluk2.
the study of synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus, a brain area involved in learning and in memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the loss of GluK2 leads to a transient decrease in the amplitude of EPSCs in the CA3 pyramide, which reflects a decrease in both the number of active synapses and the quantal amplitude.
the loss of GluK2 in mice causes a deficit in the morphofunctional maturation of hippocampus CA3 synapses, which is likely to contribute to intellectual disability.
GluK1/2 heteromeric kainate receptors, in addition to their role in synaptic plasticity and memory, also play a critical role in the morphological development of hippocampal circuits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the loss of GluK2 results in a deficit in synaptic maturation that could contribute to intellectual disability.
the absence of GluK2 results in a delay in the functional and morphofunctional maturation of mf-CA3 pyramidal cells synapses.
a mutation in the GluK gene leads to a deficit in the maturation of synaptic transmission and synaptic structure during postnatal development in a model of intellectual disability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GluK1/2 heteromers are required to maintain the correct maturation of hippocampus CA3 synapses during development.
the kainate subunit GluR6/KA2 is required for proper maturation of synaptic connections in the hippocampus during early postnatal development.
a genetic mutation linked to intellectual disability can lead to a transient deficit of synaptic transmission during development, which may impact on the proper maturation of neural circuits.
